statement: Walking up a moving escalator takes 20 seconds. Standing still on the same moving escalator takes 30 seconds. How many seconds would walking up take if the escalator were switched off?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the times, 30 - 20, as if times could be subtracted like speeds.
I added the two rates as if walking and riding were two separate helpers, 1/20 + 1/30 = 1/12.
I averaged the two times, 20 and 30, as if the answer sat halfway between them.
I added the two times, 20 + 30, as if walking and riding happened one after the other.

hints: Think in escalators per second, not seconds.

Speeds add: walking on the moving escalator, your speed is your own speed plus the escalator's speed. Write each as a fraction of the escalator per second, subtract, then turn the result back into a time.
Your own speed is 1/20 - 1/30 of the escalator per second.

solutions.reliable: Measure distance in escalator lengths. Walking on the moving escalator covers 1/20 of it per second, and the escalator alone covers 1/30 per second. Your own walking speed is the difference: 1/20 - 1/30 = 3/60 - 2/60 = 1/60 per second. So walking alone takes 60 seconds. The transferable idea: speeds and rates add and subtract, times do not.
solutions.elegant: In 60 seconds, walking on the moving escalator would cover 3 escalator lengths and the escalator alone covers 2, so your own walking covers 1 length in 60 seconds.

whyOnTest: Combining motions means combining speeds, and subtracting or averaging times gives tempting wrong choices.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
